# Recommendation Engine RFC

This document proposes a redesign of the product recommendation engine. The current system uses collaborative filtering exclusively, which works well for returning users but fails for new users and new products. The proposal introduces content-based signals and a hybrid scoring layer to address these gaps while maintaining the collaborative filtering core that drives 30% of revenue.

## Current System Analysis

The existing recommendation engine is built on an implicit feedback collaborative filtering model. User interactions such as clicks, purchases, and time spent on product pages are logged as implicit signals. These signals are fed into an alternating least squares matrix factorization model that decomposes the user-item interaction matrix into latent factor vectors of dimension 128. The model is retrained nightly on a full snapshot of the interaction history from the past 90 days.

The collaborative filtering model achieves strong performance for users with sufficient interaction history. For users with more than 20 interactions, the model produces recommendations with a mean reciprocal rank of 0.34 and a recall at 10 of 0.18. These numbers are competitive with industry benchmarks for e-commerce recommendation.

However, the model degrades sharply for users with fewer than 5 interactions. For these users, the mean reciprocal rank drops to 0.08, which is barely above the random baseline of 0.05. This is the classic cold start problem: the matrix factorization model cannot compute meaningful latent vectors for users or items with insufficient interaction data. Currently, cold start users receive popularity-based recommendations, which are not personalized and have a 60% lower click-through rate than collaborative filtering recommendations.

New products face a similar cold start issue. Products added to the catalog in the past 7 days have zero interaction data, so the collaborative filtering model cannot place them in the latent space. These products are invisible to the recommendation engine until they accumulate enough organic interactions, creating a chicken-and-egg problem where new products cannot be discovered through recommendations.

## Proposed Architecture

To address the cold start problem, we propose adding a content-based filtering pathway that generates recommendations using product metadata and user profile attributes rather than interaction history. The content-based model uses product features including category, brand, price range, textual description embeddings, and image embeddings extracted from product photos. User profiles are constructed from demographic data, stated preferences collected during onboarding, and aggregated features of previously interacted products.

The content-based model architecture is a two-tower neural network. One tower encodes user profile features into a 64-dimensional vector, and the other tower encodes product features into the same 64-dimensional space. Recommendations are generated by computing the cosine similarity between the user vector and all product vectors, then returning the top-k most similar products. This architecture allows precomputing product vectors offline and performing fast approximate nearest neighbor search at serving time using FAISS.

The two-tower model is trained on the same implicit feedback data as the collaborative filtering model, but the input features are content-based rather than interaction-based. The training objective is a pairwise loss that pushes the user vector closer to interacted products and away from randomly sampled negative products. Because the model uses content features as inputs, it can generalize to new users and new products that have no interaction history, as long as their content features are available.

For the hybrid layer, we propose a learned scoring function that combines the collaborative filtering score and the content-based score for each user-product pair. The hybrid scorer is a small feed-forward network that takes as input the collaborative score, the content score, the user's interaction count, and the product's age in days. The network outputs a single relevance score used for final ranking. This design allows the hybrid scorer to learn to rely more on content-based scores for cold start cases and more on collaborative scores for established users, without requiring hard-coded switching rules.

The hybrid scorer is trained on a held-out validation set using a listwise ranking loss. This is different from the pointwise or pairwise losses used for the individual models. The listwise loss optimizes directly for the ranking metrics we care about, specifically normalized discounted cumulative gain at position 10. Training the hybrid scorer separately from the individual models allows us to update each component independently without retraining the entire pipeline.

## Training Pipeline

The collaborative filtering model continues to train nightly on the full interaction matrix. The training pipeline reads interaction logs from the data warehouse, constructs the sparse user-item matrix, and runs 50 iterations of alternating least squares. Training time is approximately 4 hours on a single GPU instance. The trained model produces 128-dimensional latent vectors for each user and each product, which are exported to the serving layer's vector store.

We identified a data quality issue in the current training pipeline during this analysis. Approximately 3% of interaction events have incorrect timestamps due to a known clock skew bug in the mobile SDK. These events are assigned to the wrong 90-day training window, introducing noise into the model. We propose fixing the clock skew upstream and adding a timestamp validation step to the training pipeline that filters events with timestamps more than 24 hours in the future.

The content-based two-tower model trains weekly on the same interaction data but uses content features as model inputs. Training takes approximately 2 hours because the model is smaller (two small neural networks versus a large matrix factorization). The product tower's weights change slowly because product metadata is relatively stable, while the user tower's weights change more rapidly as user profiles evolve. We considered training the product tower less frequently, but the implementation complexity did not justify the marginal compute savings.

Online model updates are critical for keeping recommendations fresh. The current nightly retraining cycle means that user interactions from the morning are not reflected in recommendations until the next day. We propose adding a lightweight online update mechanism that adjusts user latent vectors in real-time as new interactions arrive. The mechanism uses stochastic gradient descent to update only the user vector while keeping product vectors fixed, allowing updates in under 10 milliseconds per interaction.

The online update system requires careful design to prevent model drift. Each user vector maintains a version counter that tracks the number of online updates since the last full retrain. When the counter exceeds a threshold of 1000 updates, the user vector is flagged for priority inclusion in the next nightly retrain batch. This hybrid approach captures the freshness benefits of online learning while maintaining the stability of periodic full retraining.

## Evaluation Plan

Offline evaluation will compare the current collaborative filtering model against the proposed hybrid model using standard ranking metrics. We will use a temporal split where the last 7 days of interaction data serve as the test set and all prior data serves as the training set. Metrics include mean reciprocal rank, recall at 10, and normalized discounted cumulative gain at 10. We will report these metrics separately for cold start users with fewer than 5 interactions, warm users with 5 to 20 interactions, and established users with more than 20 interactions.

We expect the hybrid model to show the largest improvement for cold start users, moderate improvement for warm users, and roughly equivalent performance for established users. If the hybrid model shows any degradation for established users, we will investigate whether the hybrid scorer is incorrectly overweighting the content-based signal for users where collaborative filtering alone would suffice.

The A/B test will run for 4 weeks with a 50/50 traffic split between the current collaborative filtering system and the proposed hybrid system. The primary success metric is revenue per user, which captures both the click-through rate improvement and any changes in purchase behavior. Secondary metrics include click-through rate on recommendations, diversity of recommended products measured by intra-list distance, and coverage measured as the percentage of catalog products that appear in at least one user's top-10 recommendations.

Statistical significance will be assessed using a two-sided t-test with a significance level of 0.05 and a minimum detectable effect of 1% revenue change. Power analysis indicates that with our current daily active user count of 500,000, the 4-week test duration provides 95% power to detect a 1% effect. We will also monitor for novelty effects by tracking the daily treatment effect over the test duration and checking for a decay pattern.

Production monitoring after full rollout will track recommendation quality in real-time. We will deploy a shadow scoring pipeline that continuously evaluates the model's predictions against actual user interactions with a 24-hour lag. Key monitoring metrics include the model's prediction calibration, the distribution shift between training data and live serving data measured by population stability index, and the percentage of users receiving fallback popularity-based recommendations. An alert fires if the fallback rate exceeds 15% or if the prediction calibration degrades by more than 10% from baseline.
